title: Look up and give Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk a wave! The International Space Station is flying overhead

blocks.text: Science

For the next few weeks — if you have clear skies — you can watch the International Space Station fly overhead in the evenings. If you see it, you could maybe give a little wave to Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk as he whizzes by at 7.66 kilometres a second.
ISS will be visible on clear evenings over the next few weeks
For the next few weeks — if you have clear skies — you can watch the International Space Station (ISS) fly overhead in the evenings.
If you see it, you could maybe give a little wave to Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk as he whizzes by at 7.66 kilometres a second.
Kutryk is just one of seven crew members working and living on board the orbiting laboratory as part of Expedition 75.
Since arriving on the ISS on Oct. 1, Kutryk has been hard at work with various experiments and tasks, including a recent one on cardiac research.

items: Crew-13 astronauts, including Canada's Joshua Kutryk, board the ISS after trip from Earth

blocks.text: And to no one's surprise, he's also been enjoying the view.
The ISS is often visible over Canada as it orbits the Earth. But over the coming weeks it will be visible in the evening sky, rather than the early-morning passes it's been making recently.
How to find the ISS in the sky

Very simply, it will look like a very bright white dot — compared to the thousands of fainter lights you might see that are satellites — moving across the sky. It won't have any blinking lights like airplanes and it will move steadily in one direction.

Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk conducts his 1st spacewalk

blocks.text: Now you have to find out when the ISS will be passing overhead. There are a few ways you can do this.

One is heavens-above.com, an independent website that tracks various satellites and spacecraft. There, you can sign up with your location and find the ISS in a list of other visible objects. It will then provide you with a chart of times like the one below.
This chart shows the times the ISS will be visible over Toronto over the next couple of weeks. (Heavens-above.com)
When it comes to the brightness, the more negative a number, the brighter it will appear (it doesn't appear to make sense, but that's astronomy for you).
Click on the date, and it will show you a map of the night sky with a line crossing various constellations, representing the path of the ISS.
This map of the night sky shows the constellations and the path the ISS will take on this particular pass. (Heavens-above.com)
If you only see a short line near the horizon on the map, you can probably skip that date, as the ISS may be trickier to see.
If it’s a longer line, you can give it a try, so long as you have an unobstructed view.
The constellation map will also show you the local times when the ISS will be in the sky, which is incredibly helpful.

items: A spacewalk to remember: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says seeing Earth 'changed' him

blocks.text: NASA’s Spot the Station app is another great resource.

When you open the app, it should automatically detect your location. On the home screen it will provide you with a countdown to the ISS pass. The "Sightings" button will provide you with a list of upcoming passes.
It also has a feature called AR View (augmented reality), which gives you details of the sky when you hold your phone up to it — including a line showing you where the ISS will pass.
If you can find the ISS and watch it cross the sky, just think: maybe Joshua Kutryk is looking back at you.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science.
